name: Peacock Revolution

lead: The Peacock Revolution was a menswear movement, centred in the United Kingdom from the late 1950s to the mid-1970s, that moved men's clothes from sober suits to colour, floral prints and tight silhouettes. The term was coined by consumer psychologist Ernest Dichter in 1965 and popularised by George Frazier in Esquire in 1968.
For appearance, it is an early example of men using clothing and grooming as visible self-presentation, with bold fits, colour and longer hair.

paras: Men shopped at boutiques such as John Stephen's Carnaby Street shops and Michael Fish's, wearing corduroy, paisley or brocade suits, cravats, frilly shirts, kipper ties and winklepicker boots, often with longer hair.
No health risks are associated with it. Its decline came when fashion shifted back toward classic styles by the mid-1970s.

angle.text: The movement made colour, floral prints, fitted cuts, longer hair and even makeup acceptable parts of men's self-presentation. It is a historical reference for expressive men's style.

lead: The Peacock Revolution was a fashion movement from the late 1950s to the mid-1970s, mostly in the UK, in which menswear became colourful, patterned and fitted. [1]

It began with Scottish entrepreneur John Stephen opening menswear shops on Carnaby Street in 1957. Brioni's 1952 Pitti Palace show had already anticipated bright colours and elaborate waistcoats. Michael Fish, who began experimenting with floral designs at Turnbull & Asser in 1962, opened his own boutique in 1964. [1]
The look was adopted by Mods and by rock bands including the Beatles, the Rolling Stones, the Small Faces and the Who. It reached the US around 1964 and appeared in GQ by 1966. [1]
infobox: John Stephen, Michael Fish, Pierre Cardin [1]

paras: Journalist George Frazier popularised the name in 1968 Esquire columns. Christopher Gibbs introduced double-breasted waistcoats and cloth-covered buttons, and Pierre Cardin popularised the Nehru jacket; Oleg Cassini and Bill Blass also led the movement. [1]
By the mid-1960s Stephen owned fifteen Carnaby Street shops, and Soho became known for androgynous fashion. [1]

Common items included corduroy, paisley and brocade suits, cravats, frilly shirts, kipper ties and winklepicker boots, with feminine-coded elements such as floral prints, tight silhouettes, long hair and makeup. [1]

Nostalgia for 1930s fashion sparked by Bonnie and Clyde (1967) eroded the extreme styles. Glam rock revived interest in 1972-1974, but films like The Godfather and The Great Gatsby moved fashion toward classic elegance, and John T. Molloy's Dress for Success (1975) marked a return to conservative dressing. [1]
Its legacy includes more diverse menswear, a smaller role for the suit and growing demand for grooming products. [1]
